summary: Specifies conventions for using the Walnut Digital Signature Algorithm (WalnutDSA) with COSE. WalnutDSA is described as a lightweight, quantum-resistant signature scheme based on group theory, aimed at constrained environments. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A way to sign small messages that is meant to be easy on tiny devices and hard for future quantum computers to forge.

questions: how does walnutdsa compare to rsa
subtitle: A lightweight, quantum-resistant signature algorithm for small devices.

tldr.problem: Quantum computers could break the RSA and elliptic curve signatures used everywhere today. Meanwhile, IoT and constrained devices need lightweight signatures that still work on 8- and 16-bit processors.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9021 specifies how to use WalnutDSA, a signature algorithm based on group theory, with COSE (CBOR Object Signing and Encryption). WalnutDSA is quantum-resistant and extremely efficient to verify on small processors.
tldr.outcome: The specification allows IoT devices to sign and verify messages using a post-quantum signature algorithm with minimal code and memory, providing forward security against hypothetical future quantum computers.

today: RFC 9021 is an Informational RFC published in May 2021. It provides a way to use WalnutDSA with COSE for post-quantum signature protection. Although not endorsed by the IETF, WalnutDSA is in use by organizations preparing for quantum-resistant cryptography, particularly in IoT and constrained-device applications.

sections.title: WalnutDSA and Post-Quantum Cryptography
sections.content:
WalnutDSA (Walnut Digital Signature Algorithm) is a quantum-resistant signature scheme designed to work on constrained devices. This RFC specifies how to use WalnutDSA with COSE (CBOR Object Signing and Encryption), a lightweight standard for signing and encrypting structured data.

Traditional signature algorithms like RSA and ECDSA depend on the difficulty of factoring large numbers or solving discrete logarithm problems. A sufficiently powerful quantum computer could solve these problems quickly, rendering today's digital signatures insecure. WalnutDSA, by contrast, is based on group theory and does not depend on these hard problems. It is therefore considered resistant to post-quantum attacks.

The main advantage of WalnutDSA is efficiency. The signature verification algorithm is extremely fast and compact, even on 8- and 16-bit microcontrollers. This makes it ideal for IoT and constrained devices where processing power and memory are scarce. Unlike some quantum-resistant schemes, WalnutDSA has no state limit on the number of signatures and does not require special hash-based state management.

The IETF has not formally endorsed or evaluated WalnutDSA, but this document provides a way to use it consistently with IETF protocols and conventions, allowing multiple developers to build compatible implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Quantum computers might someday break the signature system banks use. WalnutDSA is new and quantum-proof. It is also super fast on tiny computers, so it is good for smart devices.

sections.title: Post-Quantum Threats and Solutions
sections.content:
Cryptosystems depend on hard mathematical problems. RSA depends on the hardness of factoring large composite numbers. The Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) and EdDSA depend on the discrete logarithm problem. These problems are believed to be hard for classical computers, but a large-scale quantum computer using Shor's algorithm could solve them in polynomial time, breaking all three.

The threat is not hypothetical: progress in quantum computing is accelerating, and adversaries are already storing encrypted data and signed messages today, betting that quantum computers will exist within a decade and that they can break the encryption retroactively. To protect against harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks, organizations should transition to post-quantum cryptography now.

Post-quantum cryptography algorithms are designed to resist both classical and quantum attacks. Options include lattice-based, hash-based, multivariate polynomial-based, and group-theoretic schemes. WalnutDSA is a group-theoretic approach. It offers several advantages over other post-quantum schemes: small code size for verification, fast verification on weak processors, no state management or signature limits, and relatively compact signatures (though larger than RSA or ECC).
sections.plainLanguage: Today's signature systems will break if quantum computers come. WalnutDSA will not. It is also tiny to code and fast on weak processors, so IoT devices can use it now and stay safe later.

sections.title: How WalnutDSA Works
sections.content:
WalnutDSA is built on infinite group theory, a branch of abstract algebra. The core operation is called E-multiplication, which takes a matrix, a permutation, a generator in an infinite group, and a set of T-values (numbers in a finite field) and outputs a new matrix and permutation. This operation is extremely efficient to compute, especially on small processors.

Signature verification works by iterating E-multiplication for each generator in the signature, treating the signature as a string of generators. The computation is easy because E-multiplication is designed to be simple and deterministic. Unlike RSA or ECC, there is no complex arithmetic modulo large primes; instead, the computation stays within small matrices and permutations.

A WalnutDSA key is characterized by several parameters: N (the matrix dimension, typically 10) and q (the size of the finite field, typically a Mersenne prime like 2^31 - 1 or 2^61 - 1). A public key includes two matrices and permutations that define the verification parameters. Private keys include additional secret information. The signature itself is simply a sequence of generators, packed into bytes.

WalnutDSA uses SHA-2 hash algorithms (SHA-256 or SHA-512) as part of its hash-then-sign process, following standard digital signature practices.
sections.plainLanguage: WalnutDSA multiplies simple matrices by following rules from group theory. Checking a signature means doing the multiplication on the signature and seeing if you get the right answer. The math is simple enough for tiny computers.

sections.title: Integration with COSE
sections.content:
COSE is a standard for encoding and signing structured data (JSON objects) in a compact binary format called CBOR (Concise Binary Object Representation). RFC 8152 defined COSE, and this RFC adds WalnutDSA as a signature algorithm option.

When using WalnutDSA with COSE, several requirements apply. A COSE key must include the key type kty field set to "WalnutDSA" and can optionally specify the algorithm. The key operations field (key_ops) must include "sign" for signing operations or "verify" for verification. Additional WalnutDSA-specific parameters are required, including N, q, t-values, and the matrices and permutation needed for verification.

The signature value produced is a large byte string containing the WalnutDSA signature generators. The byte string is self-describing: it includes length information and type codes that allow a verifier to parse it without additional context. This design choice makes signatures easier to verify in resource-constrained environments.

COSE messages can be signed with COSE_Sign (sign-then-authenticate) or COSE_Sign1 (single signer), and WalnutDSA works with both schemes. The use of COSE makes WalnutDSA signatures compatible with a wide ecosystem of IoT protocols and applications that already support COSE.
sections.plainLanguage: COSE is a standard way to sign data. WalnutDSA is added as an option. The signature is just a byte string that includes all the information needed to check it, so verifiers do not need extra context.

sections.title: Security Analysis and Evolution
sections.content:
WalnutDSA underwent significant cryptanalytic review after its introduction. Early versions with parameters N=8 and q=32 were found to be weak and vulnerable to several attacks: Hart et al. found a universal forgery attack, Beullens and Blackburn discovered that the public key space was too small and the encoder was flawed, researchers at Stevens Institute found a length-shortening attack, and Merz and Petit discovered an attack based on Garside Normal Form.

These attacks led to parameter updates. Current parameters (N=10, q=M31 for 128-bit security; N=10, q=M61 for 256-bit security, where M31 and M61 are Mersenne primes) render all known attacks impractical. Hart's attack runs in time 2^139 with these parameters, far beyond feasible computation. The parameters also satisfy the requirement q^(N(N-1)-1) > 2^(2*Security Level), which blocks attacks exploiting small public key spaces.

Additional defenses include a corrected message encoder and additional concealed cloaking elements in the signature, both of which increase the computational cost for attackers. The two main remaining attack families (conjugacy search and Garside normal form attacks) are both exponential and sufficiently blocked by current parameters.

Implementations MUST protect private keys and use high-quality random number generators for key generation, following the guidance in RFC 4086. The RFC notes that while the IETF has not formally evaluated WalnutDSA, users should research its security properties and make informed decisions about risk.
sections.plainLanguage: WalnutDSA had weak spots in early versions, but they were fixed. With current settings, all known attacks are too hard to try. Keep private keys secret and use good random numbers when making keys.
